engine.title: Stop buying strength that has already run
engine.body: The 4H RSI ceiling for longs was 75. Splitting every closed trade by the RSI recorded at entry showed the engine bleeding above 65 and profitable below it. The ceiling is now 65.
engine.note: Holds in both halves of the sample and at every cut point tested (60, 65, 70), so it is not one lucky threshold. The threshold was still chosen from this sample, so treat the size as an upper bound.

engine.title: A break-even stop would not have helped
engine.body: The median losing trade was +1.44R in profit before it reversed, and 59% touched a full +1R first. That looks like an obvious fix: move the stop to entry once price pays 1R. Re-walking every trade bar by bar, with winners subject to the same rule, says otherwise.
engine.note: The first version of this test only altered losers, which guarantees a positive answer. Correcting it reversed the conclusion. Nothing tested cleared one standard error, so no stop rule was adopted.

engine.title: Trades were being closed at prices that never traded
engine.body: The grader had never resolved a single trade — an exception was being swallowed silently — leaving a fallback path that could book an exit at a bar from before the signal existed. Every closed trade was re-graded against bars that actually printed.
evidence: exits corrected to a real price
engine.note: This moved the headline number against me. It is published anyway, because the earlier number was not real. Pre-correction data is kept in the repo rather than deleted.

engine.title: A first target must pay back the risk
engine.body: T1 was whichever structural level sat nearest the entry, with no distance test. One signal shipped a T1 worth 0.19R against its own stop, printed beside an R:R of 2.41 quoted off T2. T1 must now return at least 1R.

chess.title: Time Management
chess.body: Chess is a timed game. Use 70-80% of your clock in complex positions, blitz transitions and endgames you know. Common mistake: spending 15 minutes in the opening, then rushing in the critical middlegame. Rule: if a position is complicated and you see candidate moves, spend the time here — not in simple positions. Clock is a resource, not just a constraint.

wisdom.title: Simplicity is the Path to Happiness
wisdom.body: Happiness research consistently shows: strong relationships + meaningful work + enough (not excessive) money = high life satisfaction. You're already building all three. Don't confuse complexity for progress. The man who simplifies wins. Less decisions, less noise, less comparison.

book.author: Andy Grove
book.chapter: The Most Valuable Output of a Manager
book.lesson: Andy Grove, Intel CEO, wrote the definitive book on management. His central insight: the output of a manager is the output of their team and the teams they influence. You are not paid to do your own work well — you are paid to maximise the output of those around you. The most leveraged activity for a manager: training and coaching. One hour of coaching that makes 10 people 10% more effective is worth 10 times more than 10 hours of personal output. His concept of 'managerial leverage' — activities that multiply the output of many — is the framework for deciding how to spend every hour.
book.key_quote: A manager's productivity is measured by the productivity they enable in others, not by their own output.
book.action: As a future financial controller: identify one skill you could teach someone on your team that would multiply your collective output.
crux: A manager's output is the output of their organisation plus the organisations they influence.
Managerial leverage = output ÷ time spent. Optimise for leverage, not effort.
Highest-leverage activities: training, and setting direction that many people then act on.
Production has three constraints everywhere: quality, cost, delivery time.
Inspect at the earliest, cheapest stage. Fixing at the end costs orders of magnitude more.
Indicators must come in pairs — one for output, one for the quality you might sacrifice for it.
Meetings are the medium of managerial work. A bad meeting is a process failure, not a waste of time in general.
One-on-ones are the highest-leverage meeting. The subordinate sets the agenda.
Decisions should be made at the lowest level with both knowledge and responsibility.
Aim for peer decision-making, then clear commitment even from dissenters.
Task-relevant maturity determines management style: low TRM needs structure, high TRM needs delegation.
Performance reviews exist to improve performance, not to rank people.
Three motivators when money is sufficient: competence, achievement, and self-actualisation.
learnings: Leverage is the only useful lens on how a manager spends an hour.
Paired indicators stop you optimising one number into a disaster.
Training your team is not overhead. It is the highest-return activity available.
Catch problems at the cheapest stage — the value-add curve is brutal.
examples: Grove's breakfast-factory model teaches limiting-step scheduling, quality gates, and capacity planning with eggs and toast.
Intel's move out of memory into microprocessors was executed through middle managers reallocating capacity before senior leadership formally decided.
Grove taught a class himself for years — one lecture, hundreds of managers, permanent leverage.
adapt: FP&A leverage: build the model once so 20 people read it right, instead of answering 20 questions.
Pair every metric: signals sent AND measured expectancy. One alone produced 180 alerts.
Inspect early — type-check and lint before commit, not after deploy.
In the Dubai role, one-on-ones with the business owners will be the highest-leverage hour of the week.

minimalism.title: The Box Test
minimalism.body: Pack a category into a box and seal it. If you have not opened it in a month, you do not need what is inside. Most people cannot name the contents a week later.
minimalism.action: Box one category — cables, kitchen gadgets, old chargers. Date the box.
minimalism.label: Minimalism

etiquette.title: Say The Difficult Thing Kindly And Once
etiquette.body: Softening it into unrecognisability is not kindness — it guarantees you say it again, worse, later. Direct and warm. Once.
etiquette.action: Name one thing you have been avoiding saying. Say it plainly today.
etiquette.label: Etiquette

stillness.title: Do One Thing At A Time
stillness.body: The monastic instruction is: when walking, walk; when eating, eat. Multitasking is the belief that attention divides without loss. It does not.
stillness.action: Do the next task with nothing else open.
stillness.label: Stillness

model.title: Opportunity Cost
model.body: The real cost of anything is the best alternative you gave up. Cash sitting idle has a cost. So does a meeting. So does a project you keep alive out of habit.
model.action: Name what your largest time commitment is displacing.
model.label: Mental Model

drill.title: Reverse-Engineer A Good Model
drill.body: Take a model you admire and rebuild its structure from scratch. Copying output teaches nothing; reconstructing the logic teaches everything.

health.title: Sleep Is The Performance Lever
health.body: Under 7 hours measurably degrades reaction time, glucose control, immune function, and emotional regulation. One night at 4 hours drops next-day insulin sensitivity by around 25%. You cannot out-discipline this.
health.action: Fixed lights-out tonight. Same time tomorrow.
health.label: Health

quote.quote: I knew that if I failed I wouldn't regret that, but I knew the one thing I might regret is not trying.

lesson.lesson: Hardships often prepare ordinary people for an extraordinary destiny.

case.title: Facebook's Instagram Acquisition (2012)
case.story: Facebook bought Instagram for $1B when it had 13 employees and $0 revenue. Zuckerberg saw mobile first. Instagram is now worth $100B+.
case.lesson: Buy what threatens you before it kills you. The best M&A is strategic, not defensive.

fpna.title: Driver-Based Forecasting
fpna.body: Build forecasts on business drivers (units, headcount, utilization), not historical % growth.

cfo.title: CFO Step 3: M&A Fundamentals
cfo.body: Basic M&A literacy: DCF valuation, EV/EBITDA multiples, due diligence process, SPA (Share Purchase Agreement), earn-out structures. You don't need to be an investment banker, but you need to read a deal memo and ask smart questions.

money_hack.title: ELSS Lock-in Trick
money_hack.body: ELSS 3-year lock-in: SIP each month → each instalment unlocks separately. Best 80C option.

dubai.title: Arabic is not required. Reading it helps.
dubai.body: No finance role in the Gulf requires Arabic. But invoices, government portals and trade licences arrive in it, and being able to read a heading rather than forwarding it is a visible edge.
dubai.targets: Numbers, months, and twenty document words. That is the whole ask.
dubai.action: Learn the Arabic numerals and the words for invoice, tax, and licence.

desk.productivity: Phone in another room during deep work. Physical distance reduces urge 60%.

father.title: Narrate what you are doing
father.do: Talk through ordinary actions out loud while she watches — 'I am pouring the water, now it is warm.'
father.why: At 7 months she is mapping sound to meaning long before she can speak. Volume of directed speech is the single best-evidenced predictor of later vocabulary. Passive audio does not count; it has to be you, to her.

father.title: Read the same book again
father.do: Read one board book daily, the same one, for a week. Point at the same picture each time.
father.why: Repetition is how infants build prediction. The boredom is yours, not hers — she is learning that symbols hold steady meaning.

life_wisdom.teaching: Reality has more facets than any single viewpoint can hold. The classic image is blind men describing an elephant — each is accurate and each is incomplete.
life_wisdom.apply: In a disagreement, state the other person's position better than they did before you argue against it. If you cannot, you have not understood it yet.

life_wisdom.teaching: The first noble truth is not 'life is suffering' but that conditioned things do not stay satisfying. The promotion satisfies briefly, then resets.
life_wisdom.apply: Before chasing the next milestone, name honestly what the last one actually changed and for how long. Then decide if you still want it.

vocab.note: Useful for defending the depth of your own work, or flagging the shallowness of someone else's.

vocab.note: Independence is the point. Two reports from the same system do not corroborate anything.

speaking.title: Answer, then stop
speaking.drill: Ask yourself an interview question, answer it, and physically close your mouth. Count three seconds before adding anything.
speaking.why: Over-explaining after a complete answer is the most common interview mistake at senior level. The silence is theirs to fill.

interview_tech.q: Sales per square foot is falling but total sales are rising. Diagnose it.
interview_tech.a: You are adding space faster than sales. That is not automatically wrong — new stores ramp, so a growth phase depresses the average mechanically. Split the estate: stores open more than 24 months versus less. If mature-store density is also falling, you have a genuine productivity problem — likely range, pricing, or footfall. If mature density is flat or up and only the blended number falls, it is a mix effect and it corrects as the new stores mature. Never let a board see the blended number alone.

interview_tech.q: Describe the difference between a cash flow forecast and a liquidity plan.
interview_tech.a: The forecast is your best estimate of receipts and payments. The liquidity plan is what you do if the forecast is wrong — committed facilities, uncommitted lines, the order in which you would draw them, what you would stop spending, and how quickly you could release working capital. Boards ask for the forecast; the CFO's real job is the plan. Stress it: what happens to cash if sales fall 20% for two quarters while committed rent and payroll continue.

interview_soft.q: Why do you want to be a CFO, and why in retail?
interview_soft.a: Structure: motive, evidence, specificity. Weak answers say 'growth' and 'leadership'. Strong answer names the work: 'I want the seat where capital allocation is decided, not just reported. In FP&A I model the store investment case; the CFO decides which twelve of thirty get built. Retail because the feedback loop is daily — you see whether the decision worked in the sales line the next week, which is not true in most industries.' Then one proof point with a number attached.

interview_soft.q: How do you build a finance team, and how do you handle an underperformer?
interview_soft.a: Building: hire for one clear gap, not a generalist; define what good looks like in writing before the first review, not after. Underperformance: the honest answer is that you probably waited too long once, and learned from it. Structure — early specific feedback with examples, an agreed plan with dates, documented check-ins, and a decision at the end of it either way. The failure mode they are probing for is a manager who avoids the conversation and lets the team carry someone for a year.
